title: What they said at the time

clips.q: Tuesday’s action ends the run of Steak & Ale, a chain founded in 1966 by Dallas-based restaurant icon Norman Brinker.
Fulfilling a promise, Grand Metropolitan P.L.C. said today that it would sell Pillsbury’s Steak & Ale and Bennigan’s restaurant chains for $431 million.
clips.who: **Eric N. Berg**, The New York Times, Mar 9, 1989[^1]

clips.q: This location is now closed for business. We thank you for your continued patronage.
clips.who: **Recorded message** at the Steak and Ale on LBJ Freeway, as transcribed by the Dallas Observer, Jul 29, 2008[^11]

clips.q: To some extent, they’ve become victims of their own success—a mature category with too many units and not enough differentiation, at least in the eyes of consumers.
clips.who: **Ron Paul**, president of Technomic, Nation’s Restaurant News, Aug 11, 2008[^5]

clips.q: Bennigan’s was heavily levered and a weaker player.
clips.who: **John Glass**, Morgan Stanley Research, Nation’s Restaurant News, Jul 29, 2008[^4]

clips.q: He was the most influential person in the restaurant industry.
clips.who: **Ellen Koteff**, editor of Nation’s Restaurant News, on Norman Brinker, The New York Times, Jun 10, 2009[^2]

clips.q: Some franchised Bennigan’s locations survived the crash, but Steak and Ale was wiped out overnight.
What I’m not going to do is bring back the old Steak & Ale with the dark, compartmentalized format inside.
They were two beautiful diamonds that just needed to be polished up and brought into the 21st century to appeal to a whole new generation.
clips.who: **Paul Mangiamele**, on the two brands, The Minnesota Star Tribune, Jul 8, 2024[^36]

clips.q: I’ve always tried to make work like play and play like hell.
clips.who: **Norman Brinker**, in a 2007 interview quoted by Nation’s Restaurant News, Jun 9, 2009[^6]
